results.title: Inside the race to train robots on human work
results.author: rjetha@businessinsider.com (Rya Jetha)
results.content:
One Friday evening this summer, a private chef prepared a three-course meal — burrata salad, baked salmon, and tiramisu — for two friends and me.
The dinner was free, but there was a catch. A camera mounted on Chef Aliser Demir's baseball cap was recording everything.
Demir came to my apartment through Shift, the data-collection arm of the German startup Microagi. The startup offers free private chefs in San Francisco in exchange for first-person footage of their work. Shift offered to pay Demir, who runs a private chef business, his usual rate of $100 to $150 per person.
"I've been feeding people since I started this job," Demir said. "Now I am also feeding AI."
Demir is part of a global effort to collect data on how humans interact with the physical world, with the goal of building machines that can staff factories, clean homes, and even fight wars. Elon Musk, who is betting Tesla's future on the humanoid robot Optimus, has promoted a utopian future of "sustainable abundance," in which AI and robots make human labor largely optional.
For now, those ambitions face a problem: a massive shortage of training data. "It is widely agreed in the robotics world that data is the key bottleneck," said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies technology and industrial policy.
This is the third installment of the AI Data Grab, Business Insider's series on how human work is becoming raw material for AI — and the companies that are cashing in. So far, we've reported on how AI labs are buying up employees' emails and Slack messages, and how law firms are turning decades of human expertise into AI systems. Now, the scramble is moving into the physical world, where companies are paying people to record skills robots have yet to learn.
Contract workers in Mexico and the Philippines remotely control robots in American warehouses as they pack beauty products, recording movements so the machines can eventually do the work on their own. Other workers across the world strap cameras to their foreheads to capture first-person footage of themselves folding laundry and making hotel beds.
"This is how the great knowledge transfer happens from humans to robots," said Josh Gruenstein, CEO of Tutor Intelligence. His company operates a Massachusetts "data factory" where workers remotely control robots to generate training data.
A booming data market
Demand for robot training data is roughly 10 times higher than a year ago, Vineeth Velmurugan, who leads robot learning at the AI data startup Encord, said. Encord's customers, including Dyna Robotics and Agility Robotics, once requested 1,000 hours of annotated data. Now they want 10,000 or even 100,000, he said.
That red-hot demand for real-world data comes as robotics has become one of Silicon Valley's hottest bets. Humanoid robot makers Figure AI and Agility Robotics have fetched multibillion-dollar valuations, as have the companies developing robot "brains" such as Skild AI and Physical Intelligence.
Robotics companies raised $33.4 billion globally in the first half of this year, according to PitchBook data, surpassing the $28.7 billion raised in all of 2025. Cheaper hardware and computing, better AI models, labor shortages, and competition with China are all fueling investor interest.
But a gulf remains between robots that perform impressive demos and machines reliable enough to work an eight-hour factory shift. Robotics companies hope more training data will help, and suppliers across the world, from scrappy startups to established companies like Scale AI, Instawork, and Uber, are rushing to sell it to them.
Custom hardware is key to recording the physical world. Mecka AI, which has raised more than $120 million from investors including Sequoia and Nvidia, started with an app that paid people to record everyday activities two years ago. But the company soon ran into the limits of ordinary video.
Mecka now designs headgear and sensor-equipped gloves to "sensorize humans," CEO Josh Gao said. The equipment records movements and force, such as the pressure needed to grip a glass or crack an egg. Contractors label workplace footage before Mecka sells it to AI labs and robotics companies.
Microagi, the parent company of Shift, is expanding its collection efforts into homes and workplaces across more than 15 countries. It pays more than 35,000 people to record themselves performing physical tasks, CEO Bercan Kilic said. Shift said participants can earn up to $30 an hour and that it has paid out around $10 million in 2026.
Household chores are the most common, but unusual tasks help expose models to unfamiliar situations. One contributor in Turkey records himself repairing old jet engines in his garage, Kilic said.
Kilic's goal is to gather enough data to build robots that can work in factories and address labor shortages in Europe and the US. "If you run factories, the math is already on your desk," Kilic previously told Business Insider. "Your most experienced people retire this decade, and their replacements were never born. Reshoring only works if the robots do."
Income today, automation tomorrow
For the workers supplying that data, though, the trade-off is income today in exchange for helping build machines that could eventually automate their work.
Demir, the private chef, said he believes his work is safe. "Machines can just watch, listen, and follow instructions," he said. "They cannot feel or smell."
The economics are different in countries where labor is cheaper. Human Archive, a data collection company based in San Francisco, began building operations in India last year through partnerships with gig platforms, hotels, and plumbing and electrical businesses. It started with an app that let people record audio and first-person video. The startup now also makes custom hardware in China, including camera-equipped headsets and wrist trackers that capture movement.
Today, it operates in more than 30 countries and pays workers between $1 to $10 and "even much more," per hour, depending on how disruptive the equipment is, CEO Raj Patel said. These workers, Patel said, could earn "almost as much, or more [than their regular jobs], to just wear these devices."
Mecka and Human Archive did not say how they ensure workers' consent when collecting data through partner businesses or local contractors. Shift said participation is voluntary, and some employees at partner businesses choose not to participate. The company said it obtains explicit consent, explaining what data is collected and how it is used, including that it may be licensed to other labs for AI and robotics training.
The global competition for data work can come with a downside. It drives down wages and leaves workers with little bargaining power, said Mark Graham, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute and author of Feeding the Machine, a book about the labor behind AI. "Often the workers don't even know what they're doing," he said. "They're a very disposable appendage of a much bigger machine."
The work can also be physically taxing. One operator who remotely controls robots in US warehouses from a Texas facility previously told Business Insider that eight-hour shifts cause arm and shoulder cramps. "We even have a massage gun in the office," they said.
Will the data boom last?
The companies collecting all this data are betting that the quest to train intelligent robots will fuel demand for years to come. Research firm Mordor Intelligence projects that the broader AI training dataset market will grow from $11.9 billion this year to nearly $49.8 billion by 2031.
For robotics data suppliers, the bull case is that startups will spend a significant share of their funding on training material, said Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners.
"If scaling laws continue to work, the pie will just keep growing," he said.
But nobody knows how much data robots will need to work reliably, he added. If they need less than expected, data suppliers could lose business. If they need much more, investors could tire of paying before the robots become commercially viable.
Some are betting that demand for robot training data is nowhere near its peak. Encord's Velmurugan likens today's robot brain to that of a two-year-old, and estimates that training a robot to work in homes — one of the hardest environments because it is so unstructured — could require a dataset five times the size of YouTube. At the end of 2025, YouTube held an estimated 29 billion videos, the equivalent of 280,000 years of footage, according to research firm Omdia.
"It's hard to say how this will play out," Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley robotics professor and cofounder of warehouse robotics startup Ambi Robotics, said. "It might take five years or 50 years. And even if we had unlimited data now, I don't know if this approach will work," he said.
Training robots in virtual environments, known as simulation, could also change the equation. World Labs, a startup slated for an $8.2 billion acquisition by AMD, says it can turn a small set of recordings into simulated environments and modify them to generate more training data for robots. If the technology delivers, robotics companies could need far less data from the physical world.
But even sustained demand doesn't guarantee a profitable business.
Earlier this year, Sam Padilla shut down his robotics data startup, Eidon AI, after struggling with logistics, upfront costs, and thin margins. He compared the business to dropshipping, where retailers sell goods shipped directly by suppliers and pocket the markup — until competitors offering the same products for less squeeze their margins.
"There is a clear arbitrage opportunity to make money if you're willing to race and race to the bottom," he said. "But a technical bottleneck does not necessarily imply a good business."

results.summary:
Startups are paying thousands of workers globally to record their daily physical tasks, creating massive datasets intended to train humanoid robots for future labor in homes and factories.

### Key Points
- Companies like Microagi, Mecka AI, and Human Archive use head-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves to capture human movements, force, and physical interactions.
- Demand for robot training data has surged tenfold in the past year, with robotics firms seeking up to 100,000 hours of annotated footage to improve machine reliability.
- Global data collection efforts span over 30 countries, with workers performing tasks ranging from cooking and cleaning to repairing jet engines.
- The AI training dataset market is projected to grow from $11.9 billion this year to nearly $49.8 billion by 2031.
- Robotics companies raised $33.4 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by investor interest in automating labor and addressing workforce shortages.

### Why it Matters
The race to build functional humanoid robots is currently bottlenecked by a lack of real-world training data, turning human labor into a critical commodity for AI development. While this creates immediate income for global workers, it simultaneously accelerates the automation of the very tasks they are being paid to record.

results.title: Kimberly Who?
results.author: Ruth Marcus
results.content:
In late 2024, as Donald Trump was preparing to take office for a second time, he had to navigate a ticklish family situation. Until recently, his son Donald Trump, Jr., had been engaged to Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host who was once married to California Governor Gavin Newsom, and Guilfoyle had become a leading figure in Trump’s orbit. She spoke—or, more precisely, shouted—on his behalf at the 2020 Republican National Convention (“They want to enslave you to the weak, dependent, liberal, victim ideology, to the point that you will not recognize this country or yourself,” Guilfoyle said of Democrats) and served as the national finance chair for Trump’s campaign. Speaking at the “Save America” rally that preceded the assault on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, Guilfoyle vowed, “We will not allow the liberals and the Democrats to steal our dream or steal our election.” The conservative group Turning Point Action paid her sixty thousand dollars for the three-minute appearance. Guilfoyle was, in short, as Eric Trump said in introducing her that day, “a warrior” for Trump.
Four years later, Guilfoyle had become less helper than headache. Trump, Jr., had been seen with another woman, a Palm Beach socialite to whom he is now married, and the couple’s engagement was called off. “I had to get her out of here,” Trump reportedly told people. (The White House has denied that Trump made this statement.) The solution: naming Guilfoyle Ambassador to Greece, a country with which she had no clear ties—her mother is from Puerto Rico, her father from Ireland—but that became, or so it appeared, a convenient place to stash the inconvenient ex.
Those who had paid attention to Guilfoyle’s past might have questioned her diplomatic skills. She was forced to leave Fox in 2018 over allegations of questionable workplace behavior. Two years later, my colleague Jane Mayer reported on the details: one of Guilfoyle’s assistants had accused her of repeated sexual harassment. The assistant, Mayer wrote, claimed to have been subject to “degrading, abusive, and sexually inappropriate behavior; among other things, she said that she was frequently required to work at Guilfoyle’s New York apartment while the Fox host displayed herself naked, and was shown photographs of the genitalia of men with whom Guilfoyle had had sexual relations.” (Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing.) Fox paid “upward of four million dollars” to settle the complaint.
On Tuesday, Guilfoyle was forced to resign from the ambassadorship a year into the post, for problems of a different nature: financial, not sexual, although her provocative attire as Ambassador also drew attention. (Among other fashion choices, Guilfoyle, who travels with a stylist, wore a see-through black lace dress to a Thanksgiving dinner hosted by the American-Hellenic Chamber of Commerce.) The Wall Street Journal had published a devastating trio of stories about Guilfoyle’s behavior on the job. First came a piece in late September about Guilfoyle’s unusually dogged advocacy on behalf of a Greek construction firm, the Aktor Group, which was seeking to break into the energy business; Christos Marafatsos, a top lobbyist for the company, “has attended so many of her meetings that some foreign officials mistook him for her chief of staff,” the Journal wrote. (Aktor and attorneys for Guilfoyle have denied any improprieties.) Then, last week, the Journal reported on Guilfoyle’s beseeching a Trump donor to wire her a hundred thousand dollars to pay her American Express bill in advance of her confirmation hearing. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle texted the donor, Eric Deters, adding a prayer-hands emoji. Deters, a Kentucky lawyer and former congressional candidate, had already paid Guilfoyle three hundred thousand dollars; among other things he sought a meeting with the commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service to discuss his tax problems. “As of this memo, I have not received one favor,” Deters wrote. “I am not naive or a sucker. I need results.”
Guilfoyle, a lawyer and a former prosecutor—she overlapped with Kamala Harris in the San Francisco district attorney’s office—understood the risk posed by Deters’s digital trail. “Stop papering all these things,” she warned, advising Deters to call her on Signal instead. “It’s really dangerous.” Deters ultimately balked at the AmEx payment. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce,” he told Guilfoyle. (Guilfoyle has suggested the texts were generated by A.I. and said, “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”)
The Journal’s final blow, on Saturday, described how Guilfoyle accepted luxury travel, including from a Greek shipping magnate who hosted Guilfoyle on his private jet and paid her bill at the Four Seasons Hotel George V, in Paris, while she was in town to attend his wife’s fashion show. Lobbying an unnamed U.S. businessman to secure an invitation to a dinner at the World Economic Forum in Davos in honor of Eric Trump, Guilfoyle promised, “I’m going to make you a lot of fucking money,” according to a recording reviewed by the Journal.
In March, celebrating Greek Independence Day at the White House, Trump described Guilfoyle as “a person I know very, very well” and “an inspiration to a lot of people.” On Tuesday, that relationship was significantly downgraded. “She wasn’t a member of my family,” Trump told reporters. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.” Kimberly who? That new chilliness was no surprise. Guilfoyle was guilty of what is, to Trump, a capital offense: her reported grift may have been comparatively small, but it failed to benefit the President and, indeed, made him look bad. Guilfoyle joined a very short list of Trump Administration officials whose ethical offenses were deemed serious enough to warrant expulsion. The other leading example from Trump’s second Administration is the former Secretary of Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, who erred, among other things, by spending two hundred and twenty million dollars in a taxpayer-funded campaign featuring the Secretary, on horseback, in front of Mt. Rushmore. Noem’s mistake was not so much promoting herself as failing to promote her boss—and, for good measure, asserting that he had been aware of her spending.
The paradox of Trump Administration corruption is that the most egregious offenders—the President chief among them—operate in plain sight and on a grand scale. They don’t fret, to borrow Guilfoyle’s verb, about “papering” the evidence; they consider themselves, perhaps with good reason, immune from consequences. To borrow from Nixon’s answer to David Frost, when the President does it, that means it is not grifting. Trump imposed some constraints on his own and his immediate family’s dealings during his first term—he promised, for example, that the Trump Organization would not conduct business abroad—but these limits, such as they were, have been shrugged off in the second. As Trump explained to the Times in January, “I found out that nobody cared. . . . I got absolutely no credit for it.”
My colleague David Kirkpatrick calculated that during the first year of his second term, Trump and his family leveraged the Presidency to make more than four billion dollars, dealing in cryptocurrency, foreign real-estate investments, and prediction markets. That total does not include the potential value of Trump’s collusive “settlement” of a private lawsuit against the I.R.S. for the leak of his tax information; as part of the arrangement, the government agreed that Trump, his family, and his companies would be immune from back taxes and penalties. Meanwhile, the President’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is both an unpaid negotiator for the Trump Administration and the owner of an investment firm, Affinity Partners, that is almost entirely financed by Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries.
When there are consequences for Trump family members’ overreach, they tend toward the minimum. Last month, ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin had paid hundreds of thousands in expenses for the wedding celebration, in May, of Donald Trump, Jr., and his new wife, Bettina Anderson Trump, including renting out a private island and putting on a fireworks display. The President described this arrangement as “very common” and “totally allowed,” but said his son was repaying the oligarch. Contrast that seeming nonchalance with Trump’s response to reports of profiteering by James Blair and Chris LaCivita, two of his senior political advisers. On October 6th, the Times reported that, in the heat of the U.S. midterm campaign, the pair had travelled to Republika Srpska, a self-governing territory in the Balkans, to help the pro-Russia government in advance of its own elections. Blair, the former deputy White House chief of staff, and LaCivita, a co-manager of Trump’s 2024 campaign, were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars through a Washington law firm, the Times said. Trump, typically, diminished his relationship with the two men, calling them “outside consultants” who “do not work for me.” He added, “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”
Guilfoyle would seem to require particularly careful handling. Having dated Don, Jr., for years, she presumably knows a lot of Trump family and Trump business secrets. So it was something of a surprise that the White House opted not to accord her the ordinary face-saving courtesy of announcing her own departure. Instead, the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, said Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. Zacharia added, incongruously, “She has been a wonderful asset to the team.” What, one wonders, would count as a liability? ♦
results.summary:
Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as U.S. Ambassador to Greece following a series of reports detailing alleged financial misconduct, improper lobbying, and the solicitation of personal payments from donors.

### Key Points
- Reports from The Wall Street Journal alleged Guilfoyle advocated for the Aktor Group, a Greek construction firm, during official diplomatic meetings.
- Evidence surfaced of Guilfoyle texting a donor to request $100,000 to cover personal credit card debt in exchange for potential political favors.
- The investigation revealed Guilfoyle accepted luxury travel and private jet accommodations from a Greek shipping magnate while serving in her official capacity.
- President Trump distanced himself from the former ambassador, stating she was not a member of his family and had only dated his son in the past.
- White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed that Guilfoyle was asked to resign from her post after one year of service.

### Why it Matters
The swift removal of a high-profile political ally highlights the Trump administration's selective approach to enforcing ethical standards when personal scandals threaten the President's public image. While the administration continues to face broader scrutiny regarding the intersection of family business interests and government policy, Guilfoyle’s expulsion serves as a rare instance of accountability for alleged profiteering.

results.title: Hacksaw Targets Operators With Peer-to-Peer Prediction Markets
results.author: ReadWrite
results.content:
Hacksaw Group has launched a B2B prediction-market platform for operators, entering a sector where annual global trading volume could reach about $1 trillion by 2030, according to an estimate cited in the company’s announcement.
The Stockholm-listed technology and game developer says the platform will let operators offer peer-to-peer prediction markets using Hacksaw’s technology, distribution network and operator relationships. The company says Bernstein estimated the market’s annual volume could reach that level as adoption expands; it is not a forecast of Hacksaw’s own business.
Operators keep their brands and customer relationships
The platform is designed to spare operators from building and maintaining the underlying technology themselves. They can offer prediction-market experiences within their own businesses while retaining their brands, customer relationships and user experiences, according to the Hacksaw announcement.
Hacksaw says its connected volume framework is intended to pool peer-to-peer participation across its operator network, giving participating businesses access to broader capacity from launch. The company also says it developed the platform within its existing cost base. The announcement does not specify operator customers, trading volumes, revenue or a rollout schedule.
The Malta Gaming Authority has approved an extension of Hacksaw’s existing B2B Critical Gaming Supply License to include Type 3 Gaming Services, alongside its existing Type 1 authorization. Hacksaw says the extension authorizes B2B peer-to-peer prediction-market services under Malta’s regulatory framework; it does not establish where or when individual operators will offer the product.
“Prediction markets represent a compelling new opportunity at the intersection of technology, entertainment and market participation,” said Ana Vrabic Verdir, Group CEO of Hacksaw Group.
A move into an adjacent market
Hacksaw describes the launch as an extension of its existing technology business into an adjacent category. Its stated operations span game development and distribution, with customers that include large private and state-owned iGaming operators. Prediction markets, the company explains, let participants trade on the likelihood of future events and outcomes.
The model puts Hacksaw behind operators rather than in the role of a consumer-facing exchange. That approach echoes other efforts to pair prediction-market technology with established organizations, including a prediction-market product developed with the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe. ReadWrite has also reported on infrastructure and products aimed at institutional prediction-market users.
The announcement’s $1 trillion figure is a market-wide estimate attributed to Bernstein, not a projection of Hacksaw’s share. The company has not disclosed commercial agreements or expected fees, so the scale of any contribution to its business remains unknown.
Hacksaw’s next concrete indicators will be whether operators adopt the platform and whether the company reports activity or financial results from the new service. Its shares trade on Nasdaq Stockholm under the ticker HACK.

Hacksaw Group has launched a B2B peer-to-peer prediction-market platform, allowing iGaming operators to integrate event-based trading technology while maintaining their own brand identity and customer relationships.

### Key Points
- The Malta Gaming Authority granted Hacksaw an extension to its B2B Critical Gaming Supply License to include Type 3 Gaming Services.
- The platform utilizes a connected volume framework to pool participation across the company’s existing network of iGaming operators.
- Hacksaw developed the new infrastructure within its current cost base without disclosing specific rollout schedules or initial commercial partners.
- The company cites Bernstein estimates suggesting the global prediction-market sector could reach $1 trillion in annual trading volume by 2030.
- Hacksaw Group remains a B2B technology provider and will not operate as a consumer-facing exchange for these prediction markets.

### Why it Matters
This expansion allows Hacksaw to diversify its revenue streams by entering the high-growth prediction-market sector without the overhead of managing direct consumer relationships. By providing the underlying infrastructure to established operators, the company positions itself to capture market share in an emerging category while leveraging its existing regulatory approvals and distribution network.

results.title: Your dusty Nest and Home speakers just got a surprise firmware lifeline
results.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
results.content:
What you need to know
- Google is updating older Nest speakers with firmware version 3.79.550760, which is being tested through the Home Preview Program.
- The original Google Home, Home Mini, Nest Mini, and Nest Audio are eligible for the update.
- Google expects to release the update more broadly over the next few weeks, but it hasn’t announced an exact date.
Some love is coming to a few of Google's older Nest speakers in the form of updates designed to make them more useful around the house — but don't expect a dramatic transformation from hardware that has been around for years.
The update, version 3.79.550760, is now in testing through Google's Home Preview Program. This includes the original Google Home from 2016, Home Mini, Nest Mini and Nest Audio. The Google Home Max isn’t included in this testing round.
The release comes as Google continues to refine its smart home experience, where voice commands and connected devices are supposed to work together without users having to fight their setup. It’s especially the case for older smart speakers, which still have utility for basic tasks as Google’s newer hardware and software evolve.
The original Home Mini was released in 2017, followed by the Nest Mini in 2019 and Nest Audio in 2020. These speakers can still handle everyday requests, but their age means they’re not necessarily getting the same attention as Google’s newer products. That said, better software can extend their usefulness.
For owners, the bigger question is whether these changes will just keep existing speakers ticking over or make them more reliable and convenient. Smart speakers are only as good as the assistants inside them, and Google’s software updates could help older Nest speakers remain useful, even as newer hardware and features arrive.
But software updates can only go so far. Older speakers can still manage basic smart home tasks and play audio; in other words, anyone expecting a major upgrade should temper their expectations.
Google’s latest moves prove it hasn’t totally forgotten about its older Nest lineup. That’s good news for those who would rather keep a perfectly functional speaker than replace it just to stay “current.”

Owners can join the preview
Owners who want to give it a try can go to the Google Home app, tap on their speaker, go to Settings > Device information > Preview program, and sign up if they are eligible. The firmware will install automatically overnight. Google expects to roll it out more widely over the next few weeks but hasn’t given a specific date.
There’s a separate October Google Home update too, improving Gemini for Home conversations, voice commands, weather responses and device controls in the app.

results.title: iPhone Duo's A20 Pro Chip Benchmarked Ahead of Launch
results.author: Juli Clover
results.content:
The iPhone Duo unsurprisingly offers performance similar to the iPhone 18 Pro, according to an early iPhone Duo benchmark shared on Geekbench 7. Both devices are equipped with Apple's 2nm A20 Pro chip with a 6-core CPU and a 7-core GPU.
The benchmarked iPhone Duo (iPhone19,4) is running iOS 27.1, as expected, and it had a single-core score of 3986 and a multi-core score of 11067. That's in line with multiple benchmarks collected from iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models.
Scores vary from test to test, so while the result does fall short of the top iPhone 18 Pro benchmark scores, we're only viewing a single score. The iPhone Duo has the same 6-core CPU with a 4.93GHz base frequency that's identified in iPhone 18 Pro benchmarks, and it lists 11.30GB memory, which means 12GB of RAM.
While the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro models use the same A20 Pro chip, there could be differences in real-world performance based on thermal management, the iPhone Duo's two screens vs. a single screen, and other factors.
Apple says the A20 Pro offers up to 20 percent faster CPU performance than the A19 Pro and up to 40 percent faster GPU performance. GPU speeds were not tested.
Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo will start on October 16, and a launch will follow on October 23.
results.summary:
Early Geekbench 7 benchmarks reveal that the upcoming iPhone Duo delivers performance comparable to the iPhone 18 Pro, powered by Apple’s advanced 2nm A20 Pro processor.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo features the A20 Pro chip, which includes a 6-core CPU and a 7-core GPU.
- Benchmark testing on iOS 27.1 yielded a single-core score of 3986 and a multi-core score of 11067.
- The device is equipped with 12GB of RAM, matching the memory specifications found in the iPhone 18 Pro series.
- Apple claims the A20 Pro provides up to 20 percent faster CPU performance and 40 percent faster GPU speeds than the previous A19 Pro.
- Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin on October 16, with an official retail launch scheduled for October 23.

### Why it Matters
These results confirm that Apple is maintaining consistent high-end performance across its latest hardware lineup despite the unique dual-screen design of the new model. Consumers can expect flagship-level processing power, though real-world performance may still vary due to thermal management and the demands of the device's dual-display configuration.

results.title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
results.author: Sean Hollister
results.content:
There’s a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to “Eiliko” over Wi-Fi, it’ll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn’t seem to care.
Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
Eiliko and its manufacturer, Energize Lab, are seemingly not to be trusted.
I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?”
“Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied.
Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy.
He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children.
If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums, look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras, and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools.
This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko.
When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world.
When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be.
For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.”
It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence.
In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses.
Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses.
While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.”
But it doesn’t seem like this company is particularly security-minded. Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach.
I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack.
“I have forwarded your massges [sic] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me.
After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions.
Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe.
My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat.
Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.”
But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.”
Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.”
Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.”
But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again.
“Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.”
My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously.
This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash.
results.summary:
The Eilik robot toy, manufactured by Energize Lab, contains severe security vulnerabilities that allow unauthorized access to private user conversations, personal profiles, and remote control of the devices.

### Key Points
- Security researcher Sammy Azdoufal discovered that Energize Lab stores 13 million user conversations on unprotected Chinese servers.
- The database includes sensitive personal information for over 68,000 active robots, including names, ages, and locations of more than 31,000 children.
- Hackers can remotely hijack the robot’s personality and LLM, forcing the device to speak inappropriate or harmful content to users.
- Despite company privacy policies claiming data is encrypted and deleted, researchers found unencrypted audio recordings and photos stored at public web addresses.
- Energize Lab has failed to address multiple inquiries regarding these security breaches or implement necessary patches to protect its global user base.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant privacy and safety risks associated with internet-connected toys that lack basic cybersecurity protections. The exposure of sensitive data and the ability for third parties to manipulate device behavior pose a direct threat to consumer safety, particularly for children.

results.title: Colleges Are Automating Admissions, but Their Most Time-Consuming Work Is Still Manual — And Costly
results.author: Ashish Fernando
results.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Colleges have automated the easy work (CRM, communication) while the hardest, most labor-intensive work (transcript evaluation, fraud checks) stays manual.
- Enrollment growth targets are outpacing the processing capacity needed to handle more applications.
- Admissions leaders want AI to extend staff capacity, not replace human judgment on consequential decisions.u003cbru003e
Higher education has invested in digital transformation for years. Colleges have adopted student information systems, customer relationship management platforms, online application portals and increasingly sophisticated communication tools. Yet many admissions teams still face significant operational challenges.
EDMO’s The State of Automation in Admissions Report 2026 offers a closer look at that contradiction. Our online survey of 40 higher education leaders at U.S. colleges and universities examined enrollment priorities, automation maturity, processing workloads, artificial intelligence and student communication.
The findings reveal an interesting divide. While 80% of respondents reported automating CRM and data synchronization and 75% reported automating student communication, only 12.5% reported automating transcript and credit evaluation. Identity and fraud checks were automated by just 17.5%.
These findings suggest that institutions have made considerable progress in automating routine administrative activities. However, some of the processes that require the most staff effort remain largely manual.
For business leaders beyond higher education, the distinction is important: introducing automation is not the same as removing the bottlenecks that constrain an organization.
The most difficult work is often the least automated
Among surveyed leaders, 70% identified staffing and workload as a major admissions challenge. Data silos and system integration followed at 50%, while 47.5% cited transcript and credit evaluation.
These pressures become easier to understand when looking at the processes that remain manual. Nearly two-thirds of respondents identified transcript and credit evaluation as largely manual. Document intake and indexing, along with identity and fraud checks, were each cited by 52.5%.
International transcripts present an additional challenge. Some 72.5% of respondents identified them among the most difficult documents to process, reflecting the complexity of evaluating different educational systems, grading scales and academic records.
The broader lesson is that organizations should examine where work becomes complicated, not simply where it is easiest to deploy technology.
For an admissions office, that may mean understanding how long a transcript waits for evaluation, how many times an incomplete document moves between teams and how frequently staff must correct or re-enter information.
Automating these processes requires more than digitizing documents. It requires workflows capable of managing inconsistent information, handling exceptions and connecting the systems involved.
Enrollment ambitions are moving faster than operational readiness
The survey also reveals a tension between institutional priorities and operational capacity.
Growing enrollment and reaching new markets was ranked the highest priority by 67.5% of respondents. Increasing yield and conversion emerged as the next major priority, with 55% assigning it second place.
Yet 47.5% rated their institution’s admissions automation maturity at three out of five. Budget constraints were cited as a barrier by 65%, followed closely by change management and staff readiness at 62.5%. Integration complexity affected 45%.
This combination creates a planning challenge. An institution may successfully increase applications but discover that its evaluation, verification and decision workflows cannot expand at the same pace.
That makes operational capacity an important part of any enrollment strategy.
Before committing to higher application targets, institutions should examine their processing capacity, identify their most time-consuming activities and assess whether existing systems can support additional volume.
Technology investments also need to account for staff readiness. A promising AI application offers limited practical value if it cannot integrate with existing systems or if employees lack the training and confidence to use it effectively.
Student communication is increasingly a capacity issue
Admissions operations are not limited to processing documents and making decisions. Institutions must also respond to students who need clarification about application requirements, financial aid, transfer credits and admission status.
The survey found that 47.5% of respondents reported average inquiry response times of two to 24 hours. Another 15% reported response times exceeding 24 hours.
Meanwhile, 72.5% said their institutions did not provide around-the-clock applicant support. Nearly half reported that 20–40% of student inquiries required staff intervention.
These findings raise an important question: how much time should admissions professionals spend answering repetitive questions when they also manage complex evaluations and consequential decisions?
Automated communication can handle routine requests, provide application updates and make information available outside traditional working hours. However, institutions must still establish clear escalation paths for questions that require personal assistance or professional judgment.
The objective should be to improve access to information while ensuring staff remain available for interactions where their expertise is essential.
Fraud concerns make human oversight essential
Growing fraud concerns add another dimension to admissions automation.
Within the surveyed group, 65% reported an increase in application or financial-aid fraud during the preceding two years. That included 40% who reported a significant increase and 25% who reported a somewhat increased level.
At the same time, 52.5% relied on manual identity verification, while only 15% reported using automated identity verification.
Institutions therefore face two competing pressures: processing applications more efficiently while maintaining reliable verification and appropriate safeguards.
The findings also suggest that admissions leaders are not looking to remove humans from these processes. When asked about the importance of human review of AI outcomes, 65% assigned a rating of four or five on a five-point scale.
This points toward a model in which technology assists with extracting information, identifying inconsistencies, routing exceptions and supporting administrative decisions, while people remain responsible for reviewing consequential outcomes.
For institutions introducing AI, oversight should be part of the original workflow design rather than an additional requirement introduced after deployment.
The real measure of automation is capacity
The most useful conclusion from this research is not that colleges need more AI. It is that institutions need a clearer understanding of where automation can meaningfully improve their operations.
Student communication and data synchronization are important, but automating these activities alone does not resolve the difficulties involved in evaluating transcripts, verifying applicant identities or managing complex applications.
Institutions should begin by identifying the work that consumes the most staff time, examining how information moves between systems and determining which activities require professional judgment.
They should then measure automation against operational outcomes: processing times, staff hours, exception rates, response capacity and the quality of human review.
For leaders in any industry, the principle is similar. The value of automation should not be judged simply by the number of tasks completed without human involvement. Its greater value lies in creating the capacity for people to focus on the work that matters most.
Key Takeaways
- Colleges have automated the easy work (CRM, communication) while the hardest, most labor-intensive work (transcript evaluation, fraud checks) stays manual.
- Enrollment growth targets are outpacing the processing capacity needed to handle more applications.
- Admissions leaders want AI to extend staff capacity, not replace human judgment on consequential decisions.u003cbru003e

Colleges have adopted student information systems, customer relationship management platforms, online application portals and increasingly sophisticated communication tools. Yet many admissions teams still face significant operational challenges.
EDMO’s The State of Automation in Admissions Report 2026 offers a closer look at that contradiction. Our online survey of 40 higher education leaders at U.S. colleges and universities examined enrollment priorities, automation maturity, processing workloads, artificial intelligence and student communication.
The findings reveal an interesting divide. While 80% of respondents reported automating CRM and data synchronization and 75% reported automating student communication, only 12.5% reported automating transcript and credit evaluation. Identity and fraud checks were automated by just 17.5%.

The State of Automation in Admissions Report 2026 reveals that U.S. colleges struggle to scale enrollment because labor-intensive tasks like transcript evaluation remain largely manual despite digital investments.

### Key Points
- While 80% of institutions automated CRM systems, only 12.5% have automated transcript and credit evaluations.
- Nearly 65% of surveyed leaders reported an increase in application or financial aid fraud over the last two years.
- Approximately 70% of admissions leaders identified staffing and heavy workloads as their primary operational challenges.
- Over 72% of institutions lack 24/7 applicant support, forcing staff to spend significant time on routine student inquiries.
- 65% of respondents emphasize that human oversight remains essential for reviewing AI-generated outcomes in admissions decisions.

### Why it Matters
Many institutions are prioritizing enrollment growth without first addressing the operational bottlenecks that prevent efficient application processing. By failing to automate complex tasks, colleges risk overwhelming their staff and hindering their ability to manage increased student volume effectively.

results.title: Anthropic’s AI worm research raises new fears about smart device security
results.author: Peter Hall
results.content:
Everything is a computer these days. Fridges, washing machines, televisions, and more are now outfitted with computer chips to give them new capabilities, and manufacturers called them “smart” even before ChatGPT came out. Now, though, researchers have strung 15 cheap TV boxes together to run an artificial intelligence model, raising the possibility that the computers inside these everyday gadgets could someday help spread autonomous, AI-powered malware.
On Monday Anthropic released a blog post exploring this sort of attack. Researchers at the company tested how AI models might act as computer worms, programs that move between devices and leave copies of themselves behind, among everyday household gadgets. A worm that runs on smart devices instead of relying on a data center could prove difficult to shut down. Anthropic’s experiments suggest how that might happen—though they stop short of demonstrating the full threat.
Typically, large language models (LLMs) are trained and run in data centers, which can contain hundreds of thousands of specialized chips called graphics processing units, or GPUs. “Just because you don’t have a big GPU doesn’t mean that you can’t be a host to one of these models,” says Jeffrey Ladish, founder and executive director of Palisade Research, a California-based AI safety nonprofit that studies the risk of AI systems slipping beyond human control, past malware to rogue behavior.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In recent months, researchers have experimented with various types of computer worms, stapling AI models onto them to make them adaptive and harder to kill. Here, though, the researchers explored whether an AI model itself could be distributed as the worm, spreading its weights to new devices and running across even weak chips.
"Anybody with an open-weight model, with the right prompts and by brute-force luck, can find these worms," says computer scientist Vyas Sekar.
Specifically, researchers working on Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team showed two key capabilities. First, they were able to split up a relatively small model—one from Google DeepMind’s open-weight Gemma line—across 15 TV boxes they had bought and networked themselves so that they could run the entire model by chaining these boxes together. Each individual box was too weak to run the model on its own. But LLMs can be split into layers, an arrangement in which each layer manipulates the data it receives and passes that revised data to the next layer. By giving each box the job of handling just a couple of these layers, the team was able to run Gemma entirely and get responses back from just the weak chips in these boxes.
After that, the researchers tested how an AI worm might spread across devices in a virtual sandbox. A larger model—from the Chinese start-up Z.ai—managed to get a smaller model—one of Meta’s Llama models—running on the targets. But the larger model was too large to run on those weak devices itself, and it still relied on a separate server. This means the team did not show an AI worm capable of spreading and running itself on such devices. Anthropic argues that as small models become more capable, one could eventually use both methods.
The research also raises the prospect of adaptation and improvement by suggesting that AI models could subsist on low-power devices and drift through the Internet, getting better at spreading as they go. Anthropic makes this clear in its blog post about the work, concluding that AI systems could soon be “passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves.”
Ladish believes the main lesson from the research is in how AI models could divvy up work across computers of all shapes and sizes. “Basically, compute is a resource that these models can use,” he says, pointing to everything from Apple MacBooks to data centers to everyday objects like smart TVs as possible sources of computing power if attackers can hack them.
Not everyone thinks that the experiments amount to a new kind of threat, however. “I think there’s some caution that’s needed here to make sure we talk about what capabilities are new and transformative,” says Michael Bailey, a professor studying computer systems security at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He emphasizes avoiding “fearmongering” with the lessons taken away from this kind of work. Researchers already know how insecure devices like TV boxes can be. “We already had self-replicating malware,” says Bailey. “We had botnets.”
“All of these are classical computer security threats,” adds Vyas Sekar, a professor of computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. According to Sekar, the bigger problem is that more people might be able to launch such attacks—a “democratization of being evil,” as he calls it. Sekar thinks this makes monitoring and restricting data flow between smart devices even more important.
Even the risk of hijacking raw computing power on chips is not new. Hackers have long taken over other people’s computers to mine cryptocurrency. So while smart devices could face new attacks of the kind Anthropic describes, the underlying weakness is an old one: plenty of our gadgets are already easy to commandeer.
results.summary:
Anthropic researchers demonstrated that artificial intelligence models could potentially operate as self-replicating worms by distributing their processing power across multiple low-power smart devices like networked TV boxes.

### Key Points
- Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team successfully ran a Google DeepMind Gemma model by splitting it across 15 networked, low-power TV boxes.
- The experiment explored the feasibility of AI models functioning as worms that spread and execute across everyday household gadgets.
- Researchers tested a Z.ai model’s ability to deploy Meta’s Llama models onto target devices within a virtual sandbox environment.
- Experts note that while the threat of self-replicating malware is not new, AI could lower the barrier for attackers to launch such campaigns.
- Security professionals emphasize that the underlying vulnerability remains the inherent insecurity of many consumer smart devices.

### Why it Matters
This research highlights how the proliferation of internet-connected devices creates a vast, distributed pool of computing power that could be exploited by malicious AI systems. While experts caution against alarmism, the findings suggest that future AI-driven threats may become more adaptive and difficult to contain as models become smaller and more efficient.

results.title: Samsung unveils an extremely small 256TB SSD for AI data centers
results.author: Asif Iqbal Shaik
results.content:
Last updated: October 15th, 2026 at 16:41 UTC+02:00
It has several solutions with faster efficiency and performance.
Samsung Electronics
Samsung remains the world's biggest memory chipmaker for good reason. The company continuously develops cutting-edge technologies to push the performance and efficiency of its silicon. Now, Samsung has unveiled a compact, ultra-dense 256TB SSD designed specifically for data centers.
During the Global Memory Innovation Forum 2026 in Shenzhen, China, Samsung Semiconductor introduced two next-generation enterprise drives: the BM1773 and the PM1763.
The BM1773 is an ultra-high-density QLC SSD available in capacities reaching up to an impressive 256TB, all packaged within the compact E3.S form factor.
Under the hood, the BM1773 leverages Samsung's 9th-generation high-density NAND flash (V9Q 2Tb) running across a 16-channel PCIe 5.0 architecture. It delivers sequential read speeds of up to 4.5GB/s and random write speeds of up to 50K IOPS. Compared to previous-generation QLC drives, the new SSD doubles total bytes written (TBW) endurance and is rated for 0.6 drive writes per day (DWPD).
It also features an intelligent die-failure recovery mechanism. If a single memory die fails, the drive continues operating normally rather than dropping the entire SSD into a restrictive read-only state. Security and compliance features include CNSA 2.0 support and FIPS sub-chip certification.
Samsung
The PM1763 is a performance-oriented PCIe 6.0 enterprise SSD. It reaches sequential read speeds of up to 28.4GB/s and write speeds of up to 21GB/s, doubling the speeds of previous-generation hardware. It is available in capacities ranging from 4TB to 64TB across E1.S, E3.S, and U.2 form factors.
Beyond pure speed, the drive delivers 1.8x better power efficiency than its predecessor and is tailored for modern liquid-cooling setups. Enterprise-grade security is robust, featuring CNSA 2.0, Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), SPDM, and TDISP-based encryption to secure sensitive server workloads.
Samsung also announced V10 NAND, the industry's first flash memory with more than 400 stacked layers. Compared to previous generations, V10 brings 58% higher data density, 33% faster transfer speeds, and a 25% reduction in power consumption.
Finally, the company showcased zNAND-O for edge and on-device AI workloads. Positioned as a high-speed bridge between conventional DRAM and flash storage, zNAND-O delivers 10x the data density of DRAM. This allows devices such as laptops, smartphones, and tablets to run large AI models locally at a fraction of the cost.
results.summary:
Samsung Electronics unveiled a new 256TB enterprise SSD and high-performance PCIe 6.0 storage solutions during the Global Memory Innovation Forum 2026 held in Shenzhen, China.

### Key Points
- The BM1773 QLC SSD offers 256TB capacity in an E3.S form factor using 9th-generation NAND flash and PCIe 5.0 architecture.
- Samsung’s PM1763 PCIe 6.0 enterprise SSD achieves read speeds of 28.4GB/s and features improved power efficiency for liquid-cooled servers.
- The company introduced V10 NAND, the industry's first flash memory featuring over 400 stacked layers for increased density and faster transfer speeds.
- New zNAND-O technology provides a high-speed bridge between DRAM and flash, enabling local AI model execution on smartphones and laptops.
- Enterprise drives include advanced security features such as Post-Quantum Cryptography, CNSA 2.0 support, and intelligent die-failure recovery mechanisms.

### Why it Matters
These advancements significantly increase data density and processing speeds for data centers managing the growing demands of enterprise AI workloads. By improving power efficiency and local AI capabilities, Samsung is positioning its hardware to lower operational costs while enhancing performance for next-generation computing infrastructure.

results.title: A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
results.author: Ben Thompson
results.content:
Good morning,
This week’s Stratechery Interview ended up not being an Interview, but rather a conversation with Hollywood super-agent Ari Emanuel. Emanuel is the Executive Chairman of WME Group, Executive Chair and CEO of TKO Group Holdings (the owner of UFC and WWE), and Founder of MARI, a live events and experiences company.
The occasion for this conversation née interview was the recent publication of Emanuel’s memoir, Roll the Calls, a reference to Emanuel’s relentless daily phone call routine; I got on Emanuel’s roll for the first time a couple of years ago, and quickly learned that when Emanuel wants something he gets it.
That’s a theme of his book, and of this interview: Emanuel decided he wanted to have a conversation and ask me some questions too, so that’s exactly what we did. We cover everything from the state of social networks, AI’s impact on Hollywood and the tech industry, and what skills might not just persist but become more valuable. We also discuss why Emanuel is making such a big bet on live, whether or not Hollywood is logical, and whether talking on the phone is the antidote to polarization.
As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.
On to the conversation:
A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
This interview is lightly edited for clarity and content.
Topics:
The State of Social | Roll the Calls | AI and Creativity | Buying UFC | Post-AI Tech | AI and Generational Change | MARI | Hollywood Logic

AE: Just like Apple, we’re not going to look at your data, major mistake when Tim [Cook] said that.

Right now you sort of have data on the user and you have data, broadly speaking, of what a particular product matches with and you’re matching, it’s called the two-towers approach. So you’re matching these two things together, and that’s how advertising basically works at scale, and it’s all these vector databases, all these sorts of things.

But all of Google Search, Amazon search—

Okay, I’ll throw away my script here.

You have this massive need for the generation of human desire, and you’re going to have people like you who are creating the vessels in which to sort of collect that human desire. But that means that advertising has just been between 1% and 2% of GDP, so let’s say that holds.
AE: Oh, it’s going up more.
It has gone up with digital, yeah, it’s up to between 2% and 3% now, but historically, it’s been between 1% and 2%.

Facebook.
