It took a new generation. And where, of course, “There’s a web app to do this sort of thing”, is the default assumption. You go back to the ’80s.
AE: What was the first SaaS company?
Depends how you define it, but I would say Microsoft, in that they really pioneered subscription pricing, it took a while to actually get there, that’s a business model question. I think from startups, I think Box is one of them that was very early. Poor Aaron Levie, he just got killed on his — he had such a vision for SaaS, but it was so early, it was so hard for him to raise money, that by the time he finally got that company to market, he barely owns a tiny slice of it even though he sort of helped write—
AE: He’s really smart.
Their prospectus is actually really interesting, they went out the first time, and total rejection by the market so they withdrew their S-1 and I actually talked to him about this at the time. And what came up with for the second S-1 was cohort analysis. This idea that — you need to not look at the company as a whole, because it’s going to be unprofitable, you look at a cohort, and it grows in profitability over time. And once you see that, you realize you actually want your SaaS company to be losing money, because the way monetization works, the more money you’re losing, the more your upside is actually increasing. Which ended up being — that was every S-1 that came after that had a cohort analysis in it.
AE: That’s a little history.
Yeah, a little history. But you go back to the ’80s, you had people bringing PCs to work — like toy PCs, like Commodores or Apple IIs, or even Apple I before that and that’s how the whole IBM/Windows story happens. IT administrators are like, “We want them to buy IBM, can you please make something for them?”. But even then, people were using it as a glorified typewriter. There’s just the generational component of — how are most people using AI today? As glorified search. That is the analogy to the glorified typewriter.
AE: A little bit of topspin on it, it will take a generation. I mean, my wife now — she’s designing, for her fashion line, almost everything, then giving it to designers, designers are tweaking it, it’s going back and forth, that will just become like one more iteration, “It is what it is”. But at the top end, you still need the high-end designer to make sure the tweaks are human.
The problem is the AI is sort of — it’s a probability distribution, you’re sort of definitionally getting middlebrow.
AE: You’re getting — what did George Gilder say? You’re getting the greatest average.
Right. But the other thing with AI is, if you just ask a general question, that’s what you get. This is part of my pushback on a lot of the safety stuff — AI is still a responsive entity, it responds to a prompt.
AE: As I like to say, it’s like watching television, you’re still leaning back.
The thing is, the AI will give you what you put in. And so if you talk to the AI about an agent-related question, the quality of analysis that you would get out of the AI would probably blow you away, this is really, really good. If I ask the AI an agent question, it’s going to be the most Wikipedia-esque, basic thing. I’ve talked about this, there was a friend — there was some court case that happened, I think it was something App Store related, it was relatively early on. I’m like, “It was unbelievable how good the AI analysis was”, because I was going back and forth with it, and he’s like, “Oh really? I wasn’t impressed at all”, and I looked — he had asked the AI, “What do I think about this case?”, and it was the most generic answer, it’s such a general question. Whereas I already had an angle on it, because I knew a lot about the area. But I also asked a very specific legal question about it, and then it was like very in-depth.
AE: That’s why I think there’s going to be an incredible creative unlock in our business. When Baz Luhrmann is inputting what he wants as a scene, as a shot, etc., and he’s giving it exactly what you’re saying — what he needs — or Ben Affleck, or Pete Berg, or whatever — the conversation is completely different from you doing it.
Right — I have no idea what to ask for.
AE: Yeah, and I just think there is that 5% that I do not think the AI, because it’s the greatest average, is going to be able to kind of take the next step. I don’t believe it gets past that point. I still think the human condition is needed, and that’s where the greatest value comes from.
Right. Also, for stuff that is sort of net new, and taste — taste is not a verifiable function.
MARI
That’s right. So one thing that was interesting, you mentioned the politics angle before, I want to ask you another question about your phone call thing. You mentioned you called one of your most famous people you represented — who was obviously Donald Trump, who you fired in 2016.
AE: I didn’t fire him! The President shouldn’t be making money. I can’t make money, it’s okay.
You related a phone call that you had in 2024, after he was reelected, and I love the anecdote, it was just like a very sort of back-and-forth conversation. Is he the one person in the world who likes to talk on the phone more than you?
AE: He likes to talk on the phone, he always picks up, he’s incredible on the phone. He’ll pick up, talk to you about anything, and you can say anything you want to him. Tell him your point of view on it, he’ll push back or not, he’ll take it in, he’ll say what things are that are on his mind, and you can push, have a conversation, and then he’s off the phone.
Right. Well, because you mentioned this in the context of, obviously, Dana White spoke at the Republican Convention, Elon Musk was part of the administration, you’re close to both for obvious reasons. And you said in the book, like, “Yeah, I lost the election, but I’m not going to not be friends with half the world”.
AE: Yeah, I’m not going to not talk to you.
I completely agree with, I think that’s a great sentiment. How much of that is actually intertwined with you being the phone guy? Like, how much of the feeling, like, “I can’t even relate to or connect to people on the other side”, is because people are living in text?
AE: I don’t think you can get a sense of a person unless you’re either Zooming or FaceTiming with them, or talking to them. I said it at the beginning — I don’t know if you’re joking or being serious on a text, it’s just too hard, I’m not that sophisticated, and it gets completely misinterpreted.
If I pick up the phone, you can say whatever you want to me, you can be aggressive, not aggressive, I can be aggressive, not aggressive. You know exactly who you’re talking to. Or you FaceTime, or you’re doing a Zoom — that’s human interaction. I mean, it’s a little bit distant if it’s a Zoom or a FaceTime, but it’s, you know, during COVID we had to do that but that’s how people can truly understand people and get across their opinion. A lot of times with Elon, I’m texting.
But you have a foundation of talking to him in person.
AE: A long time. But at least there’s a conversation happening, and you believe it’s familial — that you’re humans and you’re talking.
Right, it gives the benefit of the doubt. To the extent that AI comes along and wipes out digital, because everything digital is under threat, and AI is actually going to do everything digital better — things like MARI are more interesting and compelling. Not just because there’s more free time.
AE: I think the multiples on MARI are — not that they go up like AI, but are on the same path.
I hate that people have framed it as the anti-AI bet. It’s a pro-AI bet, you guys are going to consume all this other stuff.
AE: When I say — I’ve said the phrase “anti,” meaning the opposite bet of AI.
It’s like the bizarro-AI bet. Yeah.
AE: Yeah, it’s like — what’s going to happen in the world? Well, this is going to have to happen, because we’re human, we’re social animals, I think the multiples are going to go up. Not maybe in comparison, because it’s just the economics between them — but they’re going to go up in live.
Are you going to actually solve political polarization? Because digital — how much is that actually a driver of this? And people are going to get back to the real world, talking to people.
AE: Here’s my opinion about it. I think when you have live events, or live sports, or live music like Michael Rapino, it brings people from all social elements together.
I mean, one of the things my brother Rahm Emanuel is saying — he wants to bring back a requirement that people do service for the country — because it’s the way it used to be, where somebody from X neighborhood and somebody from Y neighborhood that would have never interfaced, do service to the country for 18 months and that we all kind of understand each other. When I go to a baseball game — I was at a baseball game, sitting watching the Cubs win — there was a guy next to me, he’s definitely a Republican.
It was obviously not a Brewers game, because the Cubs won.
AE: No, it wasn’t a Brewers game. We didn’t care that he was Republican and I was Democrat. We were just cheering for them, and it kind of broke all barriers and that’s hopefully the two businesses that I’m in heavily. That’s the great thing about it.
For sure and that’s very optimistic. I guess the question, though, is if you think about the MARI business model, and you go to like the Miami Open or something like that — is there also an underlying thesis that actually the rich are just very under-monetized?
AE: I think high-end experiences are only getting better, because there’s a great deal of rich people that want singular experiences. But we create environments for all. And, you know, there’s inside the tennis tournament, there’s XYZ, and outside there’s another 10,000 people watching it on all the screens. And Larry Ellison and David Ellison do it, and their event — we do it in Madrid also — where anybody can come and have an experience so I think we’re trying to optimize for all.
And what overall — is there a thesis with MARI that you can sort of systematize this delivery of live experiences, and do that at scale?
AE: So we have it broken down. There’s the sports vertical, which is our tennis tournaments, our participatory sports. We have our collectible business, which is Frieze, Barrett-Jackson, Collect-A-Con, which is our Pokémon experience. Then we have, like, a holiday — Winter Wonderland, our food festivals — all the stuff in that. And then we just executed against the theater business. So the West End and Broadway — we have 70 theaters in this company called ATG.
We think that is a kind of incredible — there hasn’t been one person on the live event side that exists. In the music space, it’s Live Nation and AEG. In live events, there are onesies and twosies, and so we’re trying to capture that. And what we do is, between taking things international when it’s a domestic thing — like Frieze, it was in London and New York. Now there’s two events in London, one in New York, now there’s two events in New York, one in Chicago, one in L.A., one in South Korea. And now we’re just — I think next month, we’re doing one in Abu Dhabi, and there’s other areas.
We’re going to do the same thing with Collect-A-Con on the Pokémon business, you saw how we’ve expanded when we had UFC — performance institutes and our fights all over the globe now. Then we do unbelievable sponsorship, site fees now, that’s what we do, so we’ve kind of got it down to a system of how we monetize the assets.
So what is next? Is it just acquiring more events, then, so you can plug into the system?
AE: It’s really taking our events, like Frieze, and we’re looking at different art fairs all over the place. Barrett-Jackson — can we expand it internationally? Other car auction businesses we can get into? Are there other things like Collect-A-Con — that’s Pokémon, are there other ones that we could do? And so we just look at them. When ATG came available, it’s the perfect kind of vertical that we didn’t have, that we wanted to have.
When you think about these events — but also do it like TKO and UFC and WWE — what do you think, from a business model perspective? Is it ticketing? Is it advertising? What’s the balance between those?
AE: It first starts with broadcast globally. Then from broadcast, you’re the sponsorship. Then where you take the events internationally, can you get site fees? Then you’re adding — there’s a customer that wants really high end, and will pay for really high end. And then there’s the general public, making sure their experience is incredible. And so those four or five stacks are how we think about the business, to maximize economics.
How does that align with the way you think about UFC and WWE?
AE: Those are all the things that it started. This concept started with the UFC and then we brought our sponsorship business, our site fee business to the WWE, our premium ticketing business, our ability — Mark Shapiro and myself — to make sure our broadcast deals, domestically, internationally, all of that.
For those broadcast rights business — are those, in the long run, going to be about driving subscribers or driving ads?
AE: I think for each company it’s different, but they’re all moving to an SVOD and AVOD service.
One of the things that we saw early on at the UFC, we knew that they were going to have to get to an AVOD — from a SaaS model to an advertising-based model and one of the greatest drivers there is sports, because it’s the greatest reality show. The Monday Night game — you don’t know what’s going to happen. Overtime, you think the Rams are going to win, the Bills won, and it’s the greatest model. It’s the same thing with our sports so it’s one of the great drivers and you now have four big competitors.
Do you have any concern about ending up in sort of monopsony situation where there’s not enough buyers?
AE: No. They’re all going to need it.
And there’s going to be a bunch of them?
AE: You’re now going to see what happens with Comcast and Apple. You have YouTube out there, I think all these models are going to change. One of the fastest things growing for David Ellison at Skydance is Pluto.
Right. Fox put together Roku and Tubi, which I thought was a great deal.
AE: So you’re going to have a lot of bidders. The one thing that’s great — and I think about this all the time — if the Lakers are $12.5 billion. Fantastic. Love the franchise.
Good story in your book about buying tickets.
AE: That’s a team. And that’s not the league. If a team is worth that, what are my four leagues worth? Because we have boxing, WWE.
Is that part of the allure of the UFC and WWE — you kind of get the whole thing?
AE: Yeah, running a league is different than running a team, they’re both very difficult to do. You know, they both have their personnel issues and management issues and etc. But, you know, Mark and I —
The difficulty is the moat.
AE: Mark and I run leagues. Those are hard things to do, as opposed to just a team. You’re thinking about different things, and if a team is worth that — what are the four leagues worth? I have a different conversation than the stock market is telling us right at this moment.
Is the sporting asset, given your whole model, that you are the most jealous of, Formula One?
AE: No! I think it’s an incredible sport.
Just all the things you’re talking about — the combination of the in-person events plus the rights, and all those sorts of things.
AE: I mean, think about it. First of all, I love golf, I love snooker. I mean, there’s a lot of sports that I love, that doesn’t mean that I want to be in business with them, or run them.
Hollywood Logic
Is there a world — just to go back historically a little bit — where you see streaming coming, and streaming shows up, and it’s actually this big boom, because it’s an extra window?
AE: At the time, remember, you had network syndication, so on the RSNs, you then had a cable window, it was incredible. And then all of a sudden Netflix came, you had a third window.
And is there a world where that actually persists?
AE: Well, I don’t think the syndication model — first of all, most shows are happening on streaming. You don’t get to 100 episodes, which was required.
But the reason they’re happening on streaming is because everyone decided they need to compete with Netflix. Instead, there’s a world where everyone accepts Netflix as the permanent third window, and actually makes more money all along instead of shooting themselves in the foot.
AE: That’s a logical conversation. But let me say the other side of this conversation. Do I think the network business goes to zero in cable? No, I don’t. So there is going to be a play. Remember, the original — when I was in the business, you needed to get to 100 episodes to get into syndication, now you’re doing 40 episodes.
That’s a lot these days.
AE: That’s like four seasons. So what’s the syndication window to that? It’s different. And Netflix is owning them, HBO is owning them, you’re just negotiating for the profit participants.
Is Hollywood logical?
AE: Yeah. That’s the only way I know — that you’ve been able to create over 100 years of great entertainment on the global scale, one of our great exports in the United States. Don’t you think?
Oh, for sure. Massive soft-power instrument.
AE: And I think it’s probably on the export basis — I might be wrong about this — probably our fifth or sixth most important export economically.
I write about media along with tech and Hollywood to a certain extent and my hit rate feels lower than it is, sort of, with just more tech companies and I hate the explanation that it’s because Hollywood acts more irrational.
AE: Not on every individual movie or television show. Because what do they say — if you’re batting .300 in baseball, you’re in the Hall of Fame. Same thing in Hollywood. So that’s, you know, there’s 66% — right — you’re screwing up.
Well, you mentioned David Ellison several times. Why is what he’s doing make sense?
AE: He believes if you change the tech — he believes that there’s going to be more consumption, economics for creating products is going to come down, that he’s going to be able to create unbelievable value in the SaaS model, and also take this direct-to-consumer business with the ad-based model that he has now, and also create vertical content on-site that he can kind of capture greater value than it currently exists. He’s the only one that will own his cloud, own his tech, etc. Netflix has AWS, I think Disney’s trying to change its tech right now.
Why do you need to own your own cloud?
AE: Well, I think he thinks — I think by owning that data, he’s going to get more understanding of the consumer and etc. We’ll see, that’s his point of view.
Can I ask you a question? Did you like the book?
I did. I was plowing through — no one cares about my personal schedule, but it’s been very fraught, but I was listening to it while driving, and I discovered on the plane I could listen at 3.5x speed and read at the same time, and it was unbelievable, I’ve actually never done this before.
AE: I do it all the time.
Both at the same time.
AE: I don’t look at the book. When I’m listening, I usually do a 3, 3.2x — you fly.
But if you’re listening and reading, you enter such a zone. I was flying — I flew here this morning from Chicago to L.A., I was shocked when we were landing. But it helped. I thought the book was very entertaining, I enjoyed it. How much did you write versus—
AE: You know, what we did is, when we started in 2016, [J.R. Moehringer] just kept on asking me questions. Then I answered all the questions. We met once a month, and every other week, every other month, and then he first met all my assistants.
I was going to ask you, how many assistants have you had?
AE: A lot. Some of them had kept journals, it was the craziest thing, then they met family members, friends and so he just compiled it, and then he and I went back as he was piecing it together. Then we were supposed to end when we first went public, but we didn’t go public, and then we just continued until it was 10 years.
What would you add if the book had come out a year later? What’s missing from it?
AE: I don’t know. The response has been kind of crazy from parents that have dyslexic kids, people that have dyslexia, people loving — like, re-understanding that being aggressive and rage, and taking agency for yourself, is a good thing, not a bad thing, because they’ve grown up in this place where you have to be delicate. It’s been crazy. So all in all, I’m completely happy to where it’s at right now.
Yeah. The bit about you know, you frame it as rage, but really just agency — forcing resolution.
AE: Yeah. I think that’s important to get to the end. I was having a conversation today about it. It’s like, why do I want to play this stupid game? Like — I know what you’re doing, you know that I know, let’s just have the conversation. You have to do this for this reason, I know that, just get to it already. I cannot stand this whole gray area. I can say I don’t like you, or I like you, and here’s what you did to me, and here’s how I feel about it, and go fuck yourself, and it’s ok.
Isn’t that, like, very — particularly on the West Coast — West Coast always strikes me as much more indirect, passive-aggressive.
AE: Oh you don’t think Wall Street or Silicon Valley is indirect?
No, Silicon Valley is. I think Wall Street’s much more direct.
AE: Oh you do?
I was thinking about the East Coast versus West Coast, you’re from Chicago.
AE: We’re pretty direct in Chicago.
Yeah. Is that the real secret?
AE: Maybe. I mean, it’s the only way I know how to do it, maybe that’s because I grew up with my mom and dad, and that’s what we did at our dinner table. Well, thank you.
I’ll remind you — we’ll have an ending, since we didn’t have a beginning, but thank you for coming on to Stratechery.
AE: (lauging) I appreciate it.

results.title: Norrsken and Nvidia to open Stockholm AI Lab for founders in 2027
results.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
results.content:
Norrsken Foundation and Nvidia will open a hub for AI startups in central Stockholm in 2027.
The Stockholm AI Lab will host a select group of European founders who use AI to address problems in climate, health, food and society, and it will also be home to Nvidia’s Stockholm office.
The lab will sit in a 1910 building at Birger Jarlsgatan 37, about 200 metres from Norrsken House Stockholm, the foundation’s first hub and global headquarters.
It will be Norrsken’s second site in the city, and founders can already apply for membership.
The project follows a pledge Norrsken made in June 2025, when it set aside a €300M AI fund for European startups using AI for social and environmental good. Norrsken now runs that programme under the name Prompt What Matters.
“What these founders need now is what every great movement needs: a place,” said Niklas Adalberth, the Klarna co-founder who set up Norrsken in 2016.
Nvidia is the lab’s founding technology partner, and in addition to its office, the chipmaker will offer AI computing power, developer tools for robotics, simulation, and life sciences, and links to Inception, its programme for startups.
The deal adds to Nvidia’s European AI push. Earlier this week, chief executive Jensen Huang said the company would put a further $2bn into European AI companies.
On the ground floor, Nvidia and Root Bio will run a demo lab. Root Bio, a Norrsken portfolio company formerly known as Agteria, uses AI to design molecules that address biological problems, such as greenhouse gas emissions.
Later demo partners will be chosen in robotics, climate, health and manufacturing.
In addition, the lab will have private offices for startups, a lounge for members and a regular programme of events.
Members will also be able to use both Stockholm sites and join Norrsken’s wider network.
Norrsken says Stockholm is already producing some of Europe’s fastest-growing AI companies.
It names Legora, Lovable, Sana, now part of Workday, and Einride, a Norrsken VC portfolio company that listed on Nasdaq in June at a $1.35bn valuation.
Besides Stockholm, Norrsken runs houses in Barcelona, Kigali, Brussels and Amsterdam, and its five funds have raised more than $1bn.

Apple enhanced Maps’ Austin layout with detailed 3D day and night renderings of landmarks such as The Paramount Theater, Sixth Street, the Texas State Capitol building and Terry Black’s BBQ. Navigation improvements include streets with lanes (including bus and bike lanes) marked and more accurate elevation.
The race venue marks the track’s turns, shows 3D versions of the grandstands and pit building, as well as the admission entry points. For instance, those attending the F1 race can get directions to COTA and see where roads have been temporarily closed or redirected for the event. But it will also guide you to the section where you’re seated and help you find race-specific areas such as bathrooms and first aid areas.
Although the F1 race is a big reason for visiting Austin, it’s just one of many things to do in the state’s capitol. For that weekend and the rest of the year, Apple has created a new curated guide by country music singer-songwriter Dylan Gossett. You’ll find the race track (where Gossett once worked), as well as his favorite bar, the Armadillo Den, and his favorite guitar store, Moon Music Pro.

results.title: One Windows setting helped me spot a fake PDF before I opened it
results.author: Oluwaseun Bamisile
results.content:
Cybercriminals are getting smarter by the day, and PDF phishing is one of the ways they try to infiltrate your PC. I almost fell victim to this a few days ago when I unknowingly downloaded a "PDF" file onto my laptop. But what saved me wasn't even the mighty Microsoft Defender. It was a simple setting in File Explorer that I've had turned on for months.
It's one of those Windows settings that's easy to overlook because it doesn't look important, and I’m pretty sure it’s disabled on your PC right now.
The "PDF" I downloaded wasn't actually a PDF
Showing file extensions revealed the real danger hiding behind a familiar icon
Last week, I received an email containing an invoice. The thing is, I was actually expecting an invoice around that time, so the message didn't seem suspicious. I downloaded the attachment without properly checking the email's contents or even verifying the sender.
I know, I know, that's poor internet security etiquette, and I take full responsibility for it. I've always advocated for protecting yourself online, but I let my guard down this time around. Thankfully, I had the File name extensions setting enabled in File Explorer, and it helped me catch something that I might otherwise have missed.
The file appeared to be named “Oluwaseun Invoice.pdf.exe”. At first, that may look like an ordinary invoice with an unnecessarily long filename. But look closely at the ending: exe. If I didn’t have the File name extensions setting turned on, it would have just appeared as “Oluwaseun Invoice.pdf”, and I might assume it’s a normal PDF file.
But the file wasn't a PDF document at all. It was a Windows executable disguised as an invoice by using a fake .pdf extension in its name. The .pdf in the middle was simply part of the filename. The final .exe extension identified the file as an executable program. And the craziest part was that the file had a PDF icon.
If I'd double-clicked the file, I could have launched a malicious program on my laptop, and this article topic might have been "How I Got Hacked by a PDF File."
Windows hides file extensions by default
Enabling one File Explorer setting makes suspicious filenames easier to spot
You would think a feature as life-saving as this would be enabled by default. But hey, it’s Windows, so it’s somehow disabled by default. At least enabling the setting is very easy.
Just open File Explorer, click View in the toolbar, hover over Show, and click File name extensions to enable the setting. If you're using Windows 10, open File Explorer, select the View tab, and check the File name extensions box.
You don't need to restart your computer, install anything, or change any security settings. Once enabled, the setting applies throughout File Explorer, making it easier to recognize the actual file types you're dealing with.
File extensions are just one part of staying safe online
Check suspicious files before opening them, and don't rely on one security feature
Turning on file extensions isn't a complete security solution. An actual malicious document can use a legitimate extension. My experience with that fake invoice was a useful reminder that even people who know a thing or two about cybersecurity can make mistakes.
So, while enabling file extensions is a great first step, there are other habits I recommend adopting. For instance, if you receive a document via email, check the actual email address and pay attention to subtle misspellings or unfamiliar domains. Even if you're expecting a document, take a moment to inspect the message and confirm that the attachment makes sense. Be very careful with files ending in .exe, .msi, .bat, .cmd, or .scr. These extensions can identify executable programs or scripts that you shouldn't run casually.
And please avoid opening suspicious files just to investigate them; I know it can be tempting, but resist the urge. If you aren’t sure about a file, delete it immediately. Also, ensure Microsoft Defender is active and up to date, as it can detect and block many malicious files before you open them. Cybersecurity is more about building small habits that make it harder for attackers to catch you off guard.
One small Windows setting could save you a big headache
I was lucky that a simple File Explorer setting helped me spot that suspicious invoice before I opened it. It was a small reminder that sometimes the most useful security features aren't the ones that make headlines.
However, enabling File name extensions won't protect you from every phishing email or malicious download. It won't replace antivirus software, careful browsing, or common sense. But it can expose a misleading filename before you make the mistake of opening it.
Because sometimes, the difference between a harmless document and a dangerous program is just a few characters at the end of a filename.
results.summary:
Enabling the File name extensions setting in Windows File Explorer helps users identify malicious executable files disguised as legitimate PDF documents, preventing potential cyberattacks and unauthorized software installations.

### Key Points
- Windows hides file extensions by default, allowing attackers to mask malicious .exe files as harmless PDF documents.
- Users can reveal true file types by selecting "File name extensions" under the "View" menu in File Explorer.
- Malicious files often use deceptive names like "Invoice.pdf.exe" to trick users into executing harmful programs.
- Security experts recommend avoiding files ending in .exe, .msi, .bat, .cmd, or .scr unless the source is verified.
- Enabling this setting is a simple, no-cost habit that adds a critical layer of visibility to basic Windows security.

### Why it Matters
This simple configuration change provides an immediate visual defense against common phishing tactics that rely on user oversight. By exposing hidden file extensions, users can verify the true nature of attachments before opening them, significantly reducing the risk of accidental malware infection.

results.title: Media Briefing: Overheard from publishers at Digiday London Media Strategies Town Hall
results.author: Jessica Davies
results.content:
This Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →
This week’s Media Briefing looks at what publisher execs discussed during Digiday’s Town Hall held in London this week, regarding new ways to measure audeince value, the risks of blocking AI crawlers and more.
- Publishing execs discuss the latest attempts to find the right engagement metrics for the AI era.
- The New York Times and The Economist join publisher AI coalition SPUR.
- 1,000: Number of jobs Netflix has cut globally, its biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
- $250 million+: The damages USA Today Co. is seeking from OpenAI.
- 100: The number of editorial roles Axel Springer could cut from The Telegrph’s newsroom.
- 25%: Amount Skydance’s shares slid after it issued around 471 million warrants, giving Paramount Skydance’s shareholders the option to buy shares in the new company.
- 1%: of users generated between 60% and 81% of combined subscription and advertising revenue, according to data from five INMA member publishers.
- Wirecutter wants to be more than a product review site built on affiliate links. The New York Times-owned brand is expanding into new verticals, story formats and editorial franchises that advertisers can sponsor to diversify its revenue and audience reach.
- The push is part of Wirecutter’s strategy to look for more ways to monetize and distribute its product recommendations, and reduce its dependence on search-driven affiliate commissions.
- Its latest software update cut off some of the biggest companies that track people across the web to target them with ads, stopping them from working in Safari altogether.
- Aditude, which helps publishers sell their ad space, reported Safari on iPhones and iPads accounts for 11.7% of the ads its customers show and 11.4% of their ad revenue.
- Many publishers execs say — despite the hype — agentic media buying remains a test-and-learn proposition, rather than a proven source of returns.
- That caution was clear in Digiday’s conversations with publishers at Advertising Week New York last week, where on-stage discussions dusted across the topic. But privately, publishers aren’t sold on its future. At least, not yet, according to heads of revenue and advertising at The Economist, Newsweek and The New York Times.
- CNN is bringing its All Access subscription service to the U.K. and Canada as part of a broader push to turn its international audience into paying subscribers.
- The timing could also help attract subscribers ahead of the U.S. midterms.
- There’s a growing bifurcation in the creator economy. While the Alix Earle’s and Mr Beast’s of the world take on the role of agencies, nano and micro creators have become media buys.
- “Brands are increasingly approaching the space just like they would traditional channels with a media mix that reflects what they’ve done historically,” said Zach Blume, co-founder and president of Portal A content production company on a recent episode of the Digiday Podcast.
As AI reshapes how audiences find and consume media, publishers are rethinking how to measure reach and make money, with no proven playbook yet. At Digiday’s Media Strategies London event on Tuesday, Oct. 13, executives weighed new ways to measure audience value, the risks of blocking AI crawlers, the uncertain economics of licensing content to LLMs, and whether agentic media trading is ready for the real world.
The event’s Town Hall was held under the Chatham House Rule: participants could share information, but speakers and their affiliations could not be identified. Here’s what was overheard.
Beyond page views: the search for an actionable measure of engagement
“Should we instead focus on visitors? If you think about it from first principles, you have human visitors and non-human visitors: agents, LLMs, bots, and so on. Should metrics therefore focus on the individual person as the fundamental unit? It’s something I think we’ve struggled with as an industry for a long time: defining what those unifying metrics should be.”
“We’re moving from page views towards engagement data. That includes unique users, the percentage of subscribers, dwell time, and conversions. It’s a combined metric rather than a single number. The challenge is how to distil that into something understandable for editorial teams. Page views were very simple: it was a big number or a small number, and people understood what that meant.”
“The challenge is the question: “So what? You’re telling me this, but what do I do now? Working out how to respond to a story’s performance and deciding what action to take as a result is really difficult, both to explain and to put into practice.”
“Tracking page hours over time is a very useful way to understand how a site is performing and to communicate that performance to editorial teams.”
“The difficulty for me is that if every publisher defines engagement differently, how easy will it be for agencies and clients to compare those definitions? My question is how we, as an industry, can establish a shared definition. Whether we call it attention or engagement, we need something that everyone can use as a common standard.”
“People might find a new metric interesting, but they’ll question whether it’s the right definition. They’ll ask how they can compare themselves with someone else using a slightly different formula.”
Blocking AI bots means weighing content control against future visibility
“We’re concerned about discoverability and what blocking might mean in the short term, but also the long-term implications for brand awareness over the next year or two. There’s some risk involved, but restricting access to information could also create scarcity and help establish a market for that content. The question is how big that market is today. If there’s a solid market, perhaps you’re willing to take more risks. Right now, I’m not sure we know whether there definitely is one.”
“One thing we’ve discovered is that the challenge isn’t just identifying bad actors. They keep changing and appearing under different names. The legitimate bots can also cause problems because they don’t always follow best practices. In some cases, we’ve potentially blocked legitimate bots accidentally because they haven’t identified themselves properly. For this to work, the legitimate bots need to be transparent and follow the right practices. That makes it easier for publishers to identify the bots they don’t want accessing their content.”
“We needed to establish that restricting LLM access to our entire website wouldn’t undermine our topical authority or prevent us from being cited when we wanted to be.”
“A lot may depend on what happens when the New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI finally goes through. That could help establish the value that needs to be exchanged for this content and create a significant shift in the market.”
“On the question of return on investment, publishers aren’t getting much traffic from LLMs at the moment. Click-through rates are minimal, and the traffic they do generate is limited. So, if you can secure a licensing deal, that’s potentially additional revenue. Of course, that depends on whether AI companies are still doing deals, because many of those discussions have slowed down.”
“My question wasn’t just about the traffic you receive. It was also about long-term discoverability. If people increasingly use AI to consume information, could you be undermining your long-term relevance by not being present in those systems?”
Publishers see a chance to reclaim programmatic ad value via agentic media trading, but need partners to test it
“We’ve started building a selling agent. It’s certainly not fully developed yet, but we’re working on it. The challenge is finding people on the other side to work with so we can test and develop it together.”
“These are difficult times, and publishers are under a lot of pressure. However, I see this as an opportunity to get ahead of the curve and potentially win back some of the value publishers have lost to the middlemen between them and advertisers, particularly DSPs and SSPs. I’m definitely seeing SSPs beginning to develop their capabilities in this area.”
“I think the market is approaching one of those moments when things could change significantly. If agentic trading develops as expected, being ahead of the curve could help us attract more advertising spend than competitors who arrive later. There’s also an internal benefit. If you’re fortunate enough to have people with the right technical skills, it gives them the opportunity to work on something exciting, new and cutting-edge rather than focusing exclusively on day-to-day operations. We have a small group of people working on it, and it’s a chance for them to build something genuinely innovative.”
“We’re trying to get it to a stage where we can bring in partners and start testing it properly.”
“Is agentic buying actually in the agencies’ interests? If agencies develop automated buying capabilities, they could potentially disintermediate other players, but they might also undermine a substantial part of their own existing business. Do we think this is genuinely going to come from agencies, or will it come from somewhere else?”
What we’ve heard
“Most recently, we had one trialist account try and access I think about a million different articles within about eight hours from 700,000 different IP addresses. So we are being scraped and our content taken all the time.”
– Fiona Spooner, managing director of consumer revenue at the Financial Times, speaking at Digiday’s Media Strategies event in London.
3 Qs with SPUR’s David Buttle on The New York Times, The Economist, and others joining the coalition
This week, The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Economist, AFP joined the Standards for Publisher Usage Rights initiative, or SPUR, alongside newspaper associations in Argentina, Brazil, and Mexico. That takes its membership to more than 80 publishers representing 20 countries.
SPUR released a new standard for tracking how AI tools use publishers’ content earlier this month.
Digiday’s Sara Guaglione caught up with SPUR co-founder David Buttle to hear what’s next.
This conversation has been edited and condensed.
Lots of major media companies have now joined the coalition. What spurred the momentum here, and what got them to join?
“You’d probably be surprised to hear that we haven’t been that active on that front before. We launched with an open letter calling on the industry to come behind the coalition, and then pretty much everything has been inbound. I think what that tells us is that SPUR is oriented around solving an acute problem that the whole industry is facing: content being taken and used without fair payment. The market – a sort of fair, liquid, vibrant market for content to fuel AI systems – doesn’t exist. But it urgently needs to exist. Consumer habits are beginning to change, and we need to create this market so that the economic foundations of journalism continue to support a vibrant media sector.”
Now that you have this additional support from new members, what’s next for SPUR?
“We’ve got a fairly detailed roadmap for the rest of this year and going into next year. On the telemetry standard side, we’re working with ecosystem partners to implement the standard. It will be live, working, delivering telemetry data in the wild very soon. So that’s hugely exciting. We’re doing quite a lot of work at the moment on this definition of machine use and the way that this kind of vector of IP loss from bots that choose not to respect publisher signals. And then further work on IP protection, where we’ve run extensive reviewing exercises. We’re aggregating the findings of those to paint a broader view of the cost to the publishing sector, where vulnerabilities may exist, to help members, non-members, everyone increase that cost.”
Are there any updates you can share on getting participation from the demand side, the tech platforms that were invited to join an advisory board? How are those conversations going?
“We’ll make an announcement when it’s fully formed. But [conversations] are really positive. We’re in conversations with all of the large platforms, and discussing with them the implementation of the telemetry standard, as well as other matters now as well. It’s moving in the right direction.”
– Sara Guaglione.
By the numbers
What we’ve covered

The next CEO at Condé Nast has their work cut out

NPR has promised no further job cuts after newsroom reorg

results.summary:
Publisher executives at Digiday’s London Town Hall discussed evolving engagement metrics, the risks of blocking AI crawlers, and the uncertain future of agentic media buying in journalism.

### Key Points
- The SPUR coalition, now representing over 80 publishers including The New York Times and The Economist, is developing standards to track AI usage of content.
- Industry leaders are shifting focus from simple page views to complex engagement data, such as dwell time and conversion rates, to better measure audience value.
- Publishers are debating the long-term impact of blocking AI bots, weighing potential content scarcity against the risk of losing search visibility and relevance.
- Media companies are exploring agentic media trading to reclaim ad revenue from intermediaries, though many view the technology as an unproven, experimental phase.
- Financial Times data highlights the scale of the scraping challenge, with one trialist account recently attempting to access one million articles via 700,000 IP addresses.

### Why it Matters
As AI fundamentally alters how audiences discover and consume information, publishers are struggling to establish new economic models and standardized metrics for success. The industry's ability to secure fair compensation for content and maintain direct relationships with readers will determine the long-term financial viability of professional journalism.

results.title: The Frist Line of Defense
results.author: Remy Porter
results.content:
We don't cover a lot of security issues here, simply because they're not usually funny. But sometimes, they are. So here's a quick hit about some recent ones.
We start with a very bad month for the Danish social security system, the Central Register of Persons (CPR). Last week, they detected a breach which exposed the personal details of 8.8m people. Per the Register article, a cybersecurity specialist correctly pointed out that treating your ID number as if it were a secret was a terrible idea in the first place, but unfortunately, so many systems have grown up around the idea that full knowledge of your state issued ID number as proof of identity, that the security expert is screaming into the wind. They're right, but it's going to take a lot to change.
Okay, Denmark's social security service was hacked. What's so funny about that?
Well, the mechanism of the hack appears to go thusly. First, third party companies have access to the database, which they can use to send notifications to their customers via CPR. That connection is secured with a password, and one of those third parties secured their account with the kind of password you'd use to protect the precious air of the planet Druidia. Also known as the kind of password some idiot would put on their luggage: "123456". (paywalled, Danish article).
The hacker accessed the system on September 10th, and spent ten days searching through the system. The intrusion wasn't detected until October 2nd, when CPR went to send an invoice to the third party company and noticed, "Boy, that's more searches than they have customers." Now, obviously, CPR should have never even allowed such a low complexity password, but also, the third party company shouldn't have used such a low security password.
Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to change the combination on my luggage.
In other news, I'm not particularly fond of blockchain stuff. Mostly, the whole distributed ledger seems like a solution in search of problems, and "trading tokens as if they're money" is the best thing anybody's been able to come up with. Back in my consulting days, when blockchains were all over the news, I was consulting with a large retailer, and they were exploring using blockchain in their supply chain. "How does that work?" I asked innocently. "It'll have blockchain in it." "Sure, but what does the blockchain get you?" "We'll be using blockchain. If there's like, an e. coli outbreak, we can trace where it came from." "Couldn't you get that out of a regular database?" "But this'll have blockchain."
In any case, blockchain companies getting hacked and having all their users' assets stolen is practically a daily occurrence. Not really notable. But a recent hack is legitimately interesting.
A company, called Ledger, sells "hardware wallets". Instead of storing your keys on some third party's servers (where it'll get hacked and you'll lose all your "money"), you store them on a hardware device that you put in a safe. It's not connected to the internet, and thus is unhackable. Or so you'd think. But if enough people are buying those devices, a supply chain attack becomes potentially very lucrative. And that's exactly what happened. Someone in the supply chain cracked a bunch of these devices open, and inserted new hardware. They attached a microcontroller to the screen leads, that allowed it to read what was on the screen (and thus detect when the screen was displaying a recovery code that could be used to access the wallet), and a cellular modem that allowed it to literally phone home with that information.
In total, these hackers walked away with the equivalent of nearly $100M in cryptocurrency.
All the devices passed through Ledger, where they were inspected before being sold. Presumably, they were sealed with tamper-resistant packaging. It's plausible that the tamperer was downstream from here and the customers didn't fully inspect the packaging. Even your most savvy user generally doesn't check that kind of thing, and I suspect a lot of these customers aren't actually all that savvy. But also, companies in the crypto space tend to be... we'll say, more eager than cautious, so I wouldn't be surprised if the tampering happened upstream and didn't get caught by their inspection process.
Security is hard in the best case. It's much harder when you're putting the final onus of security on end users who may have thousands or even millions of dollars locked behind a single key. Or when passwords are hard, so you pick an easy one to remember.

A massive data breach in Denmark’s Central Register of Persons and a sophisticated supply chain attack on Ledger hardware wallets highlight critical vulnerabilities in modern digital security infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Denmark’s Central Register of Persons suffered a breach exposing personal data for 8.8 million people after a third-party partner used the password "123456."
- The Danish system intrusion began on September 10 and remained undetected for over three weeks until anomalous search volume triggered an internal review on October 2.
- Hackers compromised Ledger hardware wallets by physically installing microcontrollers and cellular modems to intercept recovery codes, resulting in nearly $100 million in cryptocurrency theft.
- The Ledger attack bypassed standard security measures by targeting the physical supply chain, allowing attackers to exfiltrate sensitive keys despite the devices being offline.

### Why it Matters
These incidents demonstrate that even systems designed for high security are susceptible to failure due to human error, such as weak password management or physical supply chain tampering. They underscore the growing necessity for organizations to enforce strict authentication standards and for users to remain vigilant against physical hardware compromises.

results.title: After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back
results.author: Julie Appleby
results.content:
After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.
Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.
A fix for widespread fraud?
Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.
Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don't respond to outreach efforts by "around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections," said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.
Few details
Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.
"It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it's almost impossible to tell," said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. "That they are not being very transparent is telling too," she said of the administration.
The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children's Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.
Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants' providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.
Even so, how the move will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden's presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only states that use Healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.
"To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active," said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
How it played out
According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:
- The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.
- A broker was involved in the sign-up process.
- The plan had no monthly premium payment.
- The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.
Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers' outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn't respond.
Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting "an all-hands-on-deck" effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.
"Getting them to answer the phone isn't easy," he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.
Additionally, his team has been asked by insurers to help contact those targeted in the second phase of CMS' review. A recent case involved a client who needed to upload his new green card after his previous one expired, but language barriers meant that he had to take time off work to come in for agents to help with the process.
Information from a financial filing
CMS would not provide a list of the insurers it contacted, but publicly available documents show that New York-based Oscar Health was one.
In an August earnings call with analysts and investors, CEO Mark Bertolini said the company was reviewing the files and that "there are a number of cases where we've actually had contact" with people on the list. In other words, the company reached enrollees CMS had targeted over fraud concerns.
He did not specify how many it had reached. The company declined to comment for this article because it is in a voluntary "quiet period," when publicly traded companies limit disclosing information before the release of an earnings report.
Still, in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Oscar Health estimated that 250,000 to 300,000 of its members might be disenrolled because of the CMS effort. Nationally, the company had about 3 million members in the second quarter and reported strong profits.
Overall ACA enrollment has declined sharply, falling by nearly 3 million in the first few months of the year, due in large part to the expiration at the end of last year of the enhanced subsidies. The Trump administration has also taken some credit, saying its focus on weeding out improper enrollments and other changes, such as eliminating a special year-round low-income enrollment period, led to the decline.
CMS has also suspended some brokers for improper activity and barred new brokers from enrolling clients in ACA insurance on the federal exchange during the upcoming open enrollment period.
CMS did not respond to requests for data on the reasons it canceled enrollments. What percentage of enrollees were deemed ineligible due to incorrect income reporting or because they had other health coverage, such as through their jobs? How many because their ACA applications lacked immigration documents or Social Security numbers?
"Currently, there is no additional data to share," the agency's press office said.
But people outside the administration have been vocal.
"This was clearly phantom enrollees," said Paragon's Blase. He thinks more than 99% of the cancellations are of zero-premium coverage that people were signed up for by rogue call centers without their knowledge, or for people who don't exist at all.
Blase said the carriers had a big incentive to get hold of the enrollees because they would lose the subsidies they were being paid if the plans were canceled.
And for any people unfairly caught up, Blase and Trump administration officials say all they have to do to be reinstated is call the marketplace and provide their Social Security number or other missing information.
"Everyone has the political incentive for that process to be that easy," Blase said. "We're a month before the election."
But, as prior reporting has shown, it isn't always a quick process to get an ACA plan canceled or reinstated following an unauthorized sign-up or switch, even when a consumer discovers it themselves and reaches out to the marketplace.
Brokers and policy analysts note that some of the factors used to question enrollments — such as a plan's having no claims filed in a year — are not that unusual. Many people, for example, don't visit a doctor or hospital in a given year.
Insurers "want those healthy people in the insurance pool to help bring down the rates," said Ronnell Nolan, president and CEO of Health Agents for America, a trade group for health insurance agents. "We're against fraud, and CMS has allowed a lot of fraud to happen. But we don't want people who just didn't go to the doctor to be canceled."
And even with the outreach required by CMS, not everyone answers phone calls from unknown numbers or opens their mail or emails.
A recent marketing report found an average "open rate" on emails of 28.6%.
Policy experts also note that, while lack of a Social Security number on an ACA application could indicate a fake enrollee, it might also be an oversight, or the number might not be required, like for a child if the person applying is an adult who is not seeking coverage for the child.
"There will be legitimate people who don't have a claim or don't respond to an inquiry from an insurer," said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. "If the goal is to target fraudulent enrollment, what CMS did is better than tossing people at random, but is likely to miss the mark."
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.
results.summary:
The Trump administration has reinstated some of the 760,000 individuals previously removed from Affordable Care Act plans following concerns that legitimate enrollees were caught in anti-fraud sweeps.

### Key Points
- The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) initiated the cancellations by targeting accounts lacking Social Security numbers, premium payments, or recent claims.
- A second phase of the review is currently scrutinizing an additional 419,000 ACA sign-ups, with results expected by mid-to-late November.
- Insurers like Oscar Health were instructed to contact targeted enrollees, though many legitimate policyholders may have been disenrolled simply for failing to respond to outreach.
- Critics and policy experts warn that the lack of transparency regarding the cancellation criteria makes it difficult to distinguish between fraudulent activity and administrative errors.
- The federal government has also suspended certain insurance brokers and implemented stricter data-matching requirements to combat unauthorized enrollments on Healthcare.gov.

### Why it Matters
These cancellations highlight the tension between aggressive fraud prevention and the risk of stripping health coverage from vulnerable, eligible citizens. As the administration continues its review, the potential for widespread coverage gaps could significantly impact healthcare access for thousands of Americans in federal marketplace states.

results.title: An FBI arrest revives fears that U.S. tech companies are hiring spies
results.author: Elizabeth Dwoskin,Ian Duncan,Warren P. Strobel,Mohamad El Chamaa,Gerrit De Vynck and Zach Dorfman, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
results.content:
On paper, Abdulrahman Alfozan seemed like an ideal candidate for one of Silicon Valley's most coveted artificial intelligence jobs.
The Saudi national attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and landed an engineering job at Meta, according to his LinkedIn page and online records. Alfozan later secured a green card, spoke enthusiastically on a podcast about his Silicon Valley career and was invited to speak at Stanford University, all while working as a part-time partner at a venture capital fund dedicated to expanding the tech ecosystem in the Middle East. He had lived in the United States for more than a decade when he scored a mid-level role at OpenAI last year.
But Alfozan's arrest on Tuesday for allegedly planting a recording device in OpenAI's headquarters has ignited a fierce debate about the potential risks of Silicon Valley's international workforce - employees who often hail from nations seeking to rival the AI superpower status of the U.S.
Foreign nationals have long formed the backbone of the American tech industry, helping U.S. companies surpass their would-be international rivals. Last week, President Donald Trump awarded national medals to six tech titans for their contributions to American innovation. Five of them, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, were immigrants.
As countries battle to dominate AI, some top executives in Silicon Valley have argued that winning what they see as an existential arms race requires aggressively recruiting even more top talent from around the world.
As recently as April, Katrina Mulligan, a senior member of OpenAI's national security team, called for an "accelerated pathway to citizenship" for such workers, referring to foreign hires as a "national strategic asset" at an event on Capitol Hill. She estimated that a significant number of OpenAI's employees were not U.S. citizens, including Chinese nationals. Just half of the 300 top AI researchers in the world, she said, were American.
Other industry leaders - as well as some lawmakers - have long accused top-tier tech companies with many foreign workers of disadvantaging Americans and being breeding grounds for Chinese espionage. Palmer Luckey, CEO of weapons maker Anduril, and venture capitalist Shaun Maguire of Sequoia Capital took to X on Wednesday to revisit arguments that the industry should focus on hiring U.S. citizens. "Silicon Valley has operated with maximum openness and maximum naivete toward foreign tradecraft," Maguire wrote.
Alfozan's arrest and the debates it has re-ignited show how the AI boom has sharpened a fundamental tension in Silicon Valley: American firms must recruit from a global pool of talent while also protecting innovations that governments around the world are racing to develop or obtain for themselves.
The situation is getting even more complicated as competition intensifies, said Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a member of the National Security Council during the Biden administration.
"This technology is too powerful for [countries beyond the U.S. and China] to ignore, and the quickest and cheapest way to advance capabilities is to steal it," he added.
Arrests and convictions are relatively rare compared to the large numbers of foreign workers at U.S. tech firms. Much discussion focuses on workers from China, whose government has pledged to overtake the U.S. in AI. American intelligence agencies have long warned U.S. tech firms that they are targets of Chinese intelligence services.
"There are any number of countries that would want to know about the internal workings and future plans of OpenAI and its competitors," said Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think tank.
A spokesperson for OpenAI declined to comment. The company said in a statement late Tuesday that Alfozan's employment had been terminated. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)
In recent years, the Middle East has sought to become a major force in American technology. Funding from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have helped to fuel the costly AI boom, and billion-dollar investments often come with reciprocal obligations for U.S. AI companies to build advanced tech in the region.
Last year the Trump administration gave both countries access to some of the most advanced AI chips in the U.S. - reversing the Biden administration's more cautious stance.
Alfozan has not been charged with foreign espionage and the U.S. government has not said whether he was acting alone or as an agent of a foreign government.
But there are signs that the U.S. government is exploring the latter possibility, McGuire said.
The Department of Justice's press release about the incident says that the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control section, whose responsibility includes prosecuting spies, is assisting with the case. National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, in his statements on the case, said U.S. intelligence was committed to protecting America from "foreign threats."
A Washington-based Middle East expert, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid incurring wrath from Saudi Arabia, said he believed the Saudi government was almost certainly involved in some way.
"No one does this, not even for patriotism, without getting paid," said the person. And money would not be distributed without agreement by the Saudi royal court, he said. The Saudis lag behind their regional rival, the United Arab Emirates, in artificial intelligence development, he added.
A former CIA officer with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal Saudi dynamics, said that Saudi nationals working in Silicon Valley are celebrated back home. It's a "huge thing" for the Saudi government, said the former agency official, because Riyadh wants to build its own native technology talent base.
By working at a prominent Silicon Valley firm, you become a "big dog," said the former officer.
Alfozan, his wife and a third family member had booked one-way tickets to travel on Oct. 12 from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul, according to a motion filed by the government Oct. 8 in federal court and unsealed Wednesday.
The former OpenAI employee's public biography shows links to the Saudi government. Prince Khalid bin Bader al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, is a partner at RAED Ventures, which also lists Alfozan as a partner. The firm's X account has posted photos of partners hosting several high-ranking Saudi officials at events.
RAED did not respond to a request for comment.
In a podcast interview posted last month, Alfozan said he met Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, before he became the country's top leader during one of the prince's trips to Silicon Valley. Bin Salman inspired Alfozan to stay in Silicon Valley and grow his skills so that he could use them when he eventually returned to Saudi Arabia, he said in the interview.
At OpenAI on Wednesday, employees continued tense conversations about the political implications of the arrest for immigrant workers, two OpenAI employees said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions. The Justice Department said Tuesday that OpenAI determined the device was likely planted on Sept. 28. A company spokesman said it was found in a security sweep two days later.
The arrest triggered a discussion on OpenAI's internal Slack messaging platform among employees about whether the incident might increase pressure from the Trump administration on OpenAI to not hire foreign nationals, said one of the people.
In March, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, wrote in court papers that AI developer Anthropic's reliance on staff with ties to China was among the concerns that fueled the Defense Department's conflict with the AI company.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers have been seeking to tighten the government's oversight of the security risks faced by AI companies. In September, Sens. Jim Banks (R-Indiana) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) introduced a bill that would require AI companies that do business with the Pentagon to tell officials how they vet personnel and manage threats posed by insiders, and to report incidents of suspected espionage.
"While we await more details, this incident underscores the need for a commonsense notification framework for AI contractors to alert the Pentagon to a range of security threats," Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday.
Tensions inside the tech industry over hiring and security practices spilled out openly Wednesday on X.
Silicon Valley insiders recounted stories of stiff security within tech firms due to concerns about espionage from both commercial companies and foreign governments, in recent years.
Many companies have stepped up their security practices during the recent AI boom, often using the technology itself to speed up their understanding of strange behavior and patterns, according to Ryan Schonfeld, cofounder and CEO of HiveWatch, a startup that helps tech companies secure their facilities against insider threats.
"What used to be considered very sophisticated ... now is par for the course," he said.

### Key Points

results.title: Crunched commissions: India’s new insurance rules have prompted a basic rethink of the sector’s economics
results.author: Peeyush Dalmia, Abhishi Bhatia
results.content:
Insurance companies preparing to navigate the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (Irdai) proposed regulatory changes should anticipate shifts across distribution strategy, cost structure and their core platform. A comprehensive rethink of their business model, rather than incremental tweaks, could help them differentiate themselves and thrive.
A value shift away from distribution: As commissions drop, it is expected that pricing will follow and insurance ‘manufacturers’ will pass on the benefit to consumers.
The total new business or gross written premium could consequently shrink; even if the number of policies grows, it will likely not expand commensurately in the short-term to compensate for price drops.
With porting and renewal commissions set at the same level, the distributor has no reason to move a customer. While this means lower churn and better persistency for the incumbent’s book, switching may also stop working as a source of new business.
This could impact distributors in three ways—the commission percentage will drop; combined with price drops and new business drops from porting this means that absolute commissions will drop faster. The overall premium pool, and therefore value-based penetration, will also shrink in the short-term.
Distribution will undergo a paradigm shift.
First, a smaller pool rewards scale and productivity, so sub-scale intermediaries (agents and brokers) may exit or join tech-enabled platforms that ease selling.
Second, agency success becomes an AI and technology question—as income now depends on volume, not the rate, an insurer that speeds up an agent’s work wins the agent (including by making the agent sell multiple products). That means scored leads, instant quotes, pre-filled proposals, on-the-spot underwriting, an assistant answering product questions mid-conversation and automated renewal follow-ups. Hiring support teams is not an option with a lower expense ceiling.
Third, bancassurance could gravitate towards proprietary distribution. Without an opportunity to negotiate pricing, banks will look to create more market value through their subsidiaries, creating a challenge for insurers with significant third-party bancassurance business.
Fourth, the growth of direct selling depends on insurers passing savings on to customers and the channel. If insurers cut prices evenly everywhere, customers have no reason to change where they buy.
Direct grows if the savings appear in the direct and platform price, which Irdai proposals permit by barring distributors from insisting on uniform pricing and which the 5% platform fee ceiling makes affordable. Most insurers will hesitate, since it undercuts the channel that still writes most of their business.
More broadly, the basis of distribution will shift to either proprietary channels or brands and services in non-proprietary channels.
This could benefit better established brands as distributors will want to sell what is easier. Paying more for shelf space stops working when the rate is fixed. Distributors then pick on the product, systems integration, claims record and training. Insurers that bought distribution rather than earned it will feel this impact the most.
There could be an eventual consolidation of players in the market. Also, as value shifts from distributors to manufacturers, we might see large distributors either enter or take equity stakes in insurance manufacturing.
Changes in process and cost structure: Customer information must be verified before issuance and every policy names its seller. This relationship data could move to the insurer, and so would the servicing and renewal work previously supported by distributors. Combined with expense caps, this could impact cost structures.
With running costs already at 6-28% of premium value, achieving Irdai’s proposed 12.5% expense ratio while absorbing servicing costs could require changes beyond incremental budget reductions.
The core platform could be both a constraint and an opportunity: Regulatory compliance and AI-readiness require identical foundational systems—seller tagging, functional identities, audit-ready expense data and commission engines. As insurers must build compliant systems anyway, they could simultaneously create the infrastructure needed for AI. This modern core platform enables automation to achieve expense reduction targets that commission cuts alone cannot.
For India’s insurers, the next phase of growth may be determined less by product availability and more by distribution effectiveness, especially as customer acquisition becomes more competitive, expectations evolve and new digital channels emerge.
As McKinsey’s recent research report India’s New Insurance Track indicates, insurers can use AI to redesign core operating models for effective distribution. Conversational, voice-first and vernacular-enabled engagement could make processes more intuitive for advisors, while AI-enabled activity management may help frontline managers identify performance gaps earlier and focus on actions most likely to improve outcomes.
The adaptation window is short. Insurers that redesign their operating model comprehensively are likely to emerge ahead. These players could differentiate and thrive, while those that hesitate risk obsolescence.
These are the authors’ personal views.
The authors are, respectively, senior partner and associate partner in McKinsey’s Mumbai office.
results.summary:
Proposed regulatory changes by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) are forcing insurers to overhaul their distribution strategies, cost structures, and core technology platforms.

### Key Points
- Irdai’s proposed commission caps and pricing shifts are expected to reduce the total new business premium pool in the short term.

results.title: AhsayCBS Flaws Exploited to Deploy Web Shells Get New Fixes After Incomplete Patches
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Singapore-based Ahsay Backup has released security updates to address two security flaws in AhsayCBS that have been exploited by bad actors to drop web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners.
The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, which could be chained to sidestep authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems.
In a report published earlier this month, Huntress said it observed threat actors combining the two flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy web shells and cryptocurrency miners on exposed systems.
Although the vulnerabilities were initially assumed to be addressed in AhsayCBS versions 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0 released in August 2026, the software company has now confirmed that the patches did not completely plug them.
The fixes are available in the following versions -
- AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 hotfix
- AhsayCBS v9.15.2.70 hotfix
"Given the severity of these risks, we strongly urge you to take immediate action to secure your environment and protect your customer's data," Ahsay said. "After applying the hotfix, please reboot your server."
In an update, Huntress said it has "independently verified that the AhsayCBS 10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of this attack chain, which was still susceptible on previous v10 versions."
The active exploitation of the flaws has prompted the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add them to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patches by October 17, 2026.
